metadata.title: PISA 2012 Results: Excellence through Equity (Volume II) (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD PISA 2012 volume reports results based on the PISA 2012 assessment of 15-year-olds across 65 participating countries and economies. The report describes that school principal questionnaire responses are weighted so they are proportionate to the number of 15-year-olds enrolled in the school, indicating the use of sampling/coverage adjustments for school-level reporting. For student-level outcomes, the publication relies on PISA’s international sampling and quality controls, and it focuses on statistically significant differences/changes rather than providing a bespoke ML pipeline. The excerpt provided does not specify the exact student weight variable names (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or any replicate-weight method (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so the precise weighting implementation details are not extractable from the provided text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is an OECD PISA 2012 results volume that synthesizes equity-related findings rather than estimating a predictive model with a clearly defined PV-based dependent variable in the provided excerpt. PISA achievement outcomes are reported using PISA’s scaling framework, but the excerpt does not specify how plausible values were combined for any particular statistical model in this volume. Missing data handling is also not described as an explicit analytic procedure (e.g., imputation vs deletion) in the provided text; instead, the Reader’s Guide uses symbols (a/c/m/w) to denote categories of missingness or unavailable data for specific indicators.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: PISA 2012 targets 15-year-olds (aged 15 years 3 months to 16 years 2 months) who are enrolled in school and have completed at least 6 years of formal schooling. The report states that exclusions are governed by strict technical standards and that the overall exclusion rate within a country was required to be below 5% to limit distortion of national mean scores. Exclusions can occur at the school level (e.g., remote/inaccessible, very small schools, operational factors) or at the student level (e.g., intellectual disability or limited proficiency in the language of the assessment). The excerpt does not specify additional analytic subsampling beyond the PISA target population and the exclusion rules.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA 2012 Results volume (Volume II: Excellence through Equity) synthesizes cross-country evidence on equity in education opportunities and outcomes, focusing primarily on mathematics performance and its relationship with socio-economic status and other background factors. The report uses PISA’s international assessment design for 15-year-olds across 65 participating countries and economies, with paper-based tests (about two hours) and, in some countries, an additional 40 minutes of computer-based assessment. It reports key equity indicators such as the strength of the association between mathematics performance and ESCS, score-point differences across socio-economic groups, the share of “resilient” students, and patterns for immigrant students and pre-primary attendance. The publication emphasizes that PISA cannot identify causal effects of policies on outcomes, and it highlights statistically significant differences/changes only. In the provided excerpt, detailed PV-combination and missing-data analytic procedures are not specified at the model level; instead, the Reader’s Guide describes indicator-level missingness symbols and data availability conventions.
